event: Tyre besieged and taken by Alexander
date: Jan-Aug 332 BCE (Arrian: month Hekatombaion, archon Niketes)
source: Arrian, Anabasis (Greek ed. A. G. Roos via Perseus; tr. E. J. Chinnock 1884)
original_key_phrase: ἀλλὰ λίθων τε πολλῶν ἀφθονία ἦν καὶ ὕλης, ἥντινα τοῖς λίθοις ἄνωθεν ἐπεφόρουν, χάρακές τε οὐ χαλεπῶς κατεπήγνυντο ἐν τῷ πηλῷ καὶ αὐτὸς ὁ πηλὸς ξύνδεσμος τοῖς λίθοις ἐς τὸ ἐπιμένειν ἐγίγνετο.
translation: But there was an abundant supply of stones and wood, which they put on the top of the stones. Stakes were easily fixed down firmly in the mud, which itself served as a cement to the stones to hold them firm. (Chinnock)
notes: Mole materials: stones, timber, stakes, mud. Arrian does NOT say where the stones came from. I checked the Greek of 2.15-24: Old Tyre / Palaetyrus is never mentioned (the only "old" words are the "very ancient temple of Heracles" in Tyre, 2.16, and an "ancient custom", 2.24.5). Chinnock's own footnote 311 says the Old Tyre detail comes from Curtius, not Arrian.

event: Tyre besieged and taken by Alexander

source: Arrian, Anabasis (tr. mine, literal)
original_key_phrase: ἦν δὲ αὐτοῖς καὶ τὰ τείχη τὰ κατὰ τὸ χῶμα τό τε ὕψος εἰς πεντήκοντα καὶ ἑκατὸν μάλιστα πόδας ... λίθοις μεγάλοις ἐν γύψῳ κειμένοις ξυμπεπηγότα ... λίθοι πολλοὶ ἐς τὸ πέλαγος προβεβλημένοι ἐξεῖργον αὐτῶν τὴν ἐγγὺς προσβολήν ... ἐξάπτοντες οὖν βρόχους τῶν λίθων ἀπὸ τοῦ χώματος ἀνέσπων αὐτοὺς ἔξω τῆς θαλάσσης, ἔπειτα μηχαναῖς μετεωρίσαντες κατὰ βάθους ἀφίεσαν
translation: Their walls facing the mole were about 150 feet high ... built of large stones set in mortar ... many stones thrown out into the sea [in front of the walls] kept them from attacking at close range ... So, fastening nooses round the stones, they hauled them out of the sea from the mole, then lifted them with machines and dropped them into deep water.
notes: These were Tyrian defensive blocks in front of the island wall, cleared by the Macedonians and dumped in deep water; not stones from Old Tyre.

event: Tyre besieged and taken by Alexander
date: Jan-Aug 332 BCE (Arrian: month Hekatombaion, archon Niketes)
source: Arrian, Anabasis (tr. Chinnock)

Τύρος μὲν δὴ οὕτως ἑάλω ἐπὶ ἄρχοντος Νικήτου Ἀθήνησι μηνὸς Ἑκατομβαιῶνος.
translation: About 8,000 of the Tyrians were killed ... In the whole siege about 400 Macedonians were slain. ... The rest of the prisoners were reduced to slavery; all the Tyrians and mercenary troops, to the number of about 30,000, who had been captured, being sold. ... Thus then was Tyre captured in the month Hecatombaion, when Anicetus [Gk. Niketes] was archon at Athens.
notes: Amnesty for those who fled into the temple of Heracles, incl. King Azemilkos and Carthaginian envoys (2.24.5). Alexander then sacrificed and held a procession and games in the temple (2.24.6). Arrian says nothing about razing the city or leaving it empty.

event: Tyre besieged and taken by Alexander
date: Jan-Aug 332 BCE (Arrian: month Hekatombaion, archon Niketes)

translation: Immediately he demolished what was called Old Tyre and set many tens of thousands of men to work carrying stones to construct a mole two plethra in width. (Welles)
notes: SUPPORTS the claim that Alexander pulled down Old Tyre while building the mole. Literally "pulling down the so-called Old Tyre, and with many myriads carrying THE stones, he built a mole two plethra (c. 60 m) wide": the stones are linked to Old Tyre by the article and the shared sentence, not by an explicit "from". 17.40.4: the island lay 4 stades from the shore.

translation: He sent to the mountain and felling huge trees, he brought them branches and all and, placing them besides the mole, broke the force of the waves. (Welles)

event: Tyre besieged and taken by Alexander
date: Jan-Aug 332 BCE (Arrian: month Hekatombaion, archon Niketes)

translation: All except a few were cut down fighting, in number more than seven thousand. The king sold the women and children into slavery and crucified all the men of military age. These were not less than two thousand. Although most of the non-combatants had been removed to Carthage, those who remained to become captives were found to be more than thirteen thousand. ... after a resistance of seven months. ... He installed as king of Tyre a man named Ballonymus. (Welles)
notes: Tyre continued as a city with a king after the capture. Curtius (4.1.15ff.) tells the same gardener-king story about Sidon (Abdalonymus), so Diodorus may have confused the cities.

notes: The ONLY ancient source that says explicitly that the mole stones came from Old Tyre. Curtius wrote in the 1st c. CE (Claudius or Vespasian).

translation: But Tyre he besieged for seven months, with moles, and engines-of-war, and two hundred triremes by sea ... [25.2] and the Tyrians gave up the fight. So Alexander took the city on that day. (Perrin)

event: Tyre before and after: Nebuchadnezzar's siege; Tyre in the Roman period; Tyre in 1697; today
date: c. 586-573 BCE; 1st c. BCE-1st c. CE; 1697 CE; modern
source: Josephus, Against Apion (Greek ed. Niese via Perseus; tr. W. Whiston 1737)
original_key_phrase: ἐπ᾽ Ἰθωβάλου τοῦ βασιλέως ἐπολιόρκησε Ναβουχοδονόσορος τὴν Τύρον ἐπ᾽ ἔτη δεκατρία. μετὰ τοῦτον ἐβασίλευσε Βαὰλ ἔτη δέκα. μετὰ τοῦτον δικασταὶ κατεστάθησαν ... [1.158] μετεπέμψαντο Μέρβαλον ἐκ τῆς Βαβυλῶνος ... [1.159] ἑβδόμῳ μὲν γὰρ ἔτει τῆς Ναβουχοδονοσόρου βασιλείας ἤρξατο πολιορκεῖν Τύρον, τεσσαρεσκαιδεκάτῳ δ᾽ ἔτει τῆς Εἰρώμου Κῦρος ὁ Πέρσης τὸ κράτος παρέλαβεν.
translation: "Nabuchodonosor besieged Tyre for thirteen years in the days of Ithobal, their king; after him reigned Baal, ten years; after him were judges appointed, who judged the people: Ecnibalus, the son of Baslacus, two months; Chelbes, the son of Abdeus, ten months; Abbar, the high priest, three months; Mitgonus and Gerastratus, the sons of Abdelemus, were judges six years; after whom Balatorus reigned one year; after his death they sent and fetched Merbalus from Babylon, who reigned four years; after his death they sent for his brother Hirom, who reigned twenty years. Under his reign Cyrus became king of Persia." So that the whole interval is fifty-four years besides three months; for in the seventh year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar he began to besiege Tyre, and Cyrus the Persian took the kingdom in the fourteenth year of Hirom. (Whiston)
notes: Says only "besieged" (ἐπολιόρκησε); it does NOT say Tyre was taken or destroyed. Kings fetched "from Babylon" imply Babylonian overlordship. ("Seventh year" of Nebuchadnezzar as start of the siege is Josephus' own reckoning; the Greek has "6 years" for the two judges as a numeral sign.)

source: Strabo, Geography (Greek ed. Meineke via Perseus; tr. H. C. Hamilton & W. Falconer)
original_key_phrase: Τύρος δ᾽ ἐστὶν ὅλη νῆσος σχεδόν τι συνῳκισμένη ... συνῆπται δὲ χώματι πρὸς τὴν ἤπειρον, ὃ κατεσκεύασε πολιορκῶν Ἀλέξανδρος ... ἐνταῦθα δέ φασι πολυστέγους τὰς οἰκίας * ὥστε καὶ τῶν ἐν Ῥώμῃ μᾶλλον ... ἠτύχησε δὲ καὶ ὑπ᾽ Ἀλεξάνδρου πολιορκίᾳ ληφθεῖσα: ἀλλὰ τῶν τοιούτων συμφορῶν κατέστη κρείττων καὶ ἀνέλαβεν αὑτὴν τῇ τε ναυτιλίᾳ ... καὶ τοῖς πορφυρείοις ... πλουσίαν δὲ διὰ τὴν τοιαύτην ἀνδρείαν.
translation: Tyre is wholly an island, built nearly in the same manner as Aradus. It is joined to the continent by a mound, which Alexander raised, when he was besieging it. ... The houses here, it is said, consist of many stories, of more even than at Rome ... It sustained great injury when it was taken by siege by Alexander, but it rose above these misfortunes, and recovered itself both by the skill of the people in the art of navigation ... and by (the export of) purple-dyed manufactures ... the source of its wealth. Their independence was secured to them ... by the kings of Syria, but also by the Romans. (Hamilton-Falconer)
notes: Tyre in Strabo's day (late 1st c. BCE / early 1st c. CE): rebuilt, densely populated, rich, autonomous. Compare Curtius 4.4.21 (E01).

[3.4.10] ἐντεῦθεν δ᾽ ἐπορεύθησαν σταθμὸν ἕνα παρασάγγας ἓξ πρὸς τεῖχος ἔρημον μέγα ... ὄνομα δὲ ἦν τῇ πόλει Μέσπιλα: Μῆδοι δ᾽ αὐτήν ποτε ᾤκουν. [3.4.11] ... τοῦ δὲ τείχους ἡ περίοδος ἓξ παρασάγγαι. [3.4.12] ... Ζεὺς δὲ βροντῇ κατέπληξε τοὺς ἐνοικοῦντας, καὶ οὕτως ἑάλω.
translation: [3.4.7] Here was a large deserted city; its name was Larisa, and it was inhabited in ancient times by the Medes. [3.4.10] From this place they marched one stage, six parasangs, to a great stronghold, deserted and lying in ruins. The name of this city was Mespila, and it was once inhabited by the Medes. [3.4.11] ... the circuit of the wall was six parasangs. [3.4.12] ... Zeus, however, terrified the inhabitants with thunder, and thus the city was taken. (Brownson)
notes: Xenophon does NOT name Nineveh or mention Assyria; he attributes both cities to the Medes and their capture to "the king of the Persians". Equating Mespila with Nineveh and Larisa with Calah (Nimrud) is a modern identification (e.g., Brownson's footnotes), not Xenophon's statement.
